orient: Narrator: Lockwood, the next day (still 1801). Despite his cold welcome, he walks the four miles back to Wuthering Heights as snow begins to fall, and meets the rest of the household.

notes.g: Began (of weather): the afternoon started out misty and cold.
Open, wild, uncultivated land covered with heather and rough grass.
The main meal, eaten here around midday.
notes.m: Not an evening meal: Lockwood says he dines 'between twelve and one'.

notes.g: Short for Latin 'nota bene': note well, take note.

notes.t: I might be served at five
notes.g: Lockwood wanted dinner at five o'clock.
notes.n: Fashionable town people dined late in the day. His country housekeeper keeps the old rural habit of a midday dinner, and won't change.

notes.g: Like a dignified, motherly, middle-aged woman.

notes.t: taken as a fixture along with the house
notes.g: Who came with the rented house, like the built-in furniture.
notes.m: A 'fixture' is something fixed to a property that stays when it is rented or sold. Lockwood is joking.
notes.n: Remember this housekeeper. She becomes very important from Chapter IV.

notes.g: Metal buckets for carrying and holding coal by the fireplace.

notes.t: extinguished the flames with heaps of cinders
notes.g: Putting the fire out by smothering it with ashes, to clean the fireplace.
notes.n: So Lockwood's study is cold and dusty, and he goes out instead.

notes.g: A hard frost without any white frost or snow on the ground, so the earth looks dark.
The raised path paved with flagstones (see Chapter I).
Prickly fruit bushes, common in farmhouse gardens.

notes.m: 'Inmates' meant the residents of any house, not only of a prison or hospital.

notes.g: I exclaimed, silently in my head.
notes.m: 'Ejaculate' meant to exclaim suddenly (see Chapter I).

notes.g: Being cut off from other people forever.

notes.n: 'Churlish' means rude and mean-spirited. A 'churl' was originally a low-born peasant.

notes.e: if ye went to spake to him.
notes.tr: What do you want? The master's down in the fold. Go round by the end of the barn if you want to speak to him.

notes.g: Master: the head of the household (here, Heathcliff).
Fold: an enclosure or pen for sheep or cattle.

notes.n: From an old Norse word for a storehouse. Many Yorkshire dialect words come from Old Norse.

notes.tr: There's nobody but the mistress, and she won't open it even if you keep up your horrible racket until nightfall.

notes.g: The mistress: the woman of the house.
notes.n: Lockwood didn't know she existed. He uses Joseph's word for her a moment later.

notes.g: If you make; even if you make.
notes.n: 'An' meaning 'if' is very old English, found in Shakespeare too.
From the dialect verb 'flay' or 'fley', to frighten.
Strictly this should be 'who I am'. Lockwood's over-correct grammar is part of his fussy character.

notes.tr: Not me! I'll have no hand in it.

notes.g: Joseph's head, disappearing from the window.
notes.n: A joke: Lockwood can only see Joseph's head poking out of the barn window.
Driving snow is snow blown sideways by the wind, piling up in drifts.

notes.m: 'Essay' as a verb means 'try', not a piece of writing.

notes.g: A long-handled fork with two or three prongs for lifting hay.
A hand pump for drawing water from a well.
A dovecote: a small house or shelter for keeping pigeons, raised for eating.
Dried blocks of turf dug from bogs, burned as fuel on the moors.
How slowly your servants answer the door.
notes.n: A polite complaint. 'Leisure' here means unhurried.

notes.m: 'Regardless' is an adjective here, meaning 'paying no regard', not 'anyway'.

notes.g: The female pointer who attacked Lockwood in Chapter I.
notes.n: Named after the queen of the Roman gods. Lockwood calls her 'the villain'.

notes.g: Lowered herself to do something (as if it were a favour).

notes.m: 'Interview' simply meant a face-to-face meeting.

notes.t: in token of owning my acquaintance
notes.g: As a sign that she recognised me.
notes.n: 'Own' here means 'acknowledge'.

notes.g: Friendly hostess (said sarcastically: she is anything but).
A cushion in the shadows, hard to see.
notes.m: 'Obscure' here means dim or dark, not little-known.

notes.g: The mantelpiece: the shelf above a fireplace.

notes.n: Flax is a plant whose fibres are a pale yellow.

notes.g: A heart that easily falls in love.
notes.n: Lockwood thinks of himself as a romantic. Remember the girl at the seaside in Chapter I.

notes.m: 'Singularly' means remarkably.

notes.g: A person who hoards money and hates to spend or share it.

notes.n: Tea was expensive, kept in a canister, and measured out by spoon.

notes.g: In a sulk; in a fit of bad temper.
notes.m: Nothing to do with animals.

notes.t: for all the world as if

notes.g: A deadly quarrel not yet revenged.

notes.m: Here 'rude' means coarse and unpolished, more than impolite.

notes.g: Side-whiskers spread over his cheeks like a bear's fur.
Tanned and roughened by outdoor work.

notes.t: his bearing was free, almost haughty
notes.g: He carried himself confidently, almost proudly.
notes.n: So he does not act like a servant, which confuses Lockwood.
A servant would be expected to wait attentively on the lady of the house.

notes.m: Not his health.

notes.g: Stuck indoors because of bad weather.
The country boy; the young farmhand-looking man.

notes.m: A joking old use: to 'discuss' food meant to eat it, since nobody discussed anything.
'Genius' here is the Roman idea of a protective spirit of a person or place, not a very clever person.
A verb here (in-ti-MATE), not the adjective meaning 'close'.

notes.g: A guardian angel who looks after people.
notes.n: A phrase from Shakespeare's Hamlet. Heathcliff mockingly assumes Lockwood means a dead wife watching over the house.
Lockwood jokes that only old men fool themselves that young girls marry them for love.

notes.g: The country bumpkin; the uncouth peasant.
notes.m: Not a circus clown. 'Clown' originally meant a rough rustic.

notes.n: Drinking tea from a bowl instead of a cup was a mark of bad manners.
Lockwood's vanity is funny here: he insists he is not conceited, then praises himself.

notes.m: Here it leans towards 'strange', but also 'special to this situation'.

notes.t: favoured possessor of the beneficent fairy
notes.g: The lucky owner of this kind fairy (meaning her husband).
notes.n: Lockwood's flowery compliment, which goes badly wrong.

notes.m: Not 'at present, now'.

notes.g: The young woman at the Heights. Heathcliff will explain that she is his son's widow.
notes.n: Her first name isn't given yet.

notes.g: The rough young man. He has the same name as the one carved over the front door.
notes.n: So he belongs to the old Earnshaw family of the house, yet he seems to live almost like a servant.

notes.g: Hit him on the side of the head.
The sloping beams that hold up a roof.
The covered entrance of the barn.
Oatmeal boiled with water, used as cheap food for farm dogs as well as people.

notes.s: Aw wonder how yah can faishion
notes.tr: I wonder how you have the nerve to stand there doing nothing, or worse, when all of them have gone out! But you're a good-for-nothing, and it's no use talking. You'll never mend your wicked ways, but go straight to the devil, like your mother before you!
notes.n: Joseph is talking to Mrs. Heathcliff, not to Lockwood, although Lockwood thinks at first that he is.

notes.g: Bring yourself to; have the nerve to.
Snatched away, body and all, by the devil.
notes.n: A popular belief: say the devil's name carelessly and he might come for you.

notes.t: ask your abduction as a special favour
notes.g: Ask the devil to carry you off as a special favour to me.

notes.n: She is teasing Joseph's superstitious fears, pretending her book is a book of spells.

notes.t: make a clear house of it
notes.g: Get rid of everyone in the house.

notes.n: 'Providence' is God's guidance of events. She claims her witchcraft, not God, caused his pains.
A term from strict Calvinist Protestantism, which Joseph follows: the 'reprobate' are those God has rejected. She throws his own language back at him.
A Bible word (1 Corinthians 9:27), again turned against Joseph.

notes.g: Made into wax and clay figures, as in witchcraft.
notes.n: Folk magic held that you could hurt a person by damaging a little model of them.

notes.g: A kind of bleak, joyless joke.
Wet, spongy ground where you can sink.
A hollow or old pit (perhaps a quarry or mine shaft) filled with snow.
A servant at Wuthering Heights: the housekeeper who chased off the dogs in Chapter I.
Freedom to wander around the house.
The enclosed grounds around Thrushcross Grange.

notes.tr: Master, master, he's stealing the lantern!

notes.g: A small back or side gate.
Hold him! (Joseph setting the dogs on Lockwood.)

notes.n: Like 'Wolf', a name chosen to sound fierce.
Literally, the top stone of a wall. Their laughter 'tops off' his humiliation.

notes.g: Would not let me get up.
notes.m: 'Suffer' here means 'allow'.

notes.g: Sounded like King Lear in Shakespeare's play.
notes.n: Lear, raging at his daughters, threatens terrible revenges but can't say what they will be. Lockwood's empty threats are just as vague.

notes.m: Not a performer.

notes.g: Sturdy woman who runs the household.
notes.m: 'Stout' meant strong or sturdy (also plump); 'housewife' here means a housekeeper, not a married woman at home.

notes.g: Her loud scolding (a joking military image).
Going on; afoot. 'What you'll be up to next'.

notes.n: In Yorkshire speech 'fair' means 'completely, truly'.

notes.g: Necessarily; because there was no choice.

notes.m: 'Sorry' here means pitiful or wretched, not apologetic.
